attributes.body:
なくてもいい is simply the opposite of てもいい, and highlights that it is 'ok even if (A) is not done'. This usually comes across as being quite polite, and sounds like 'don't worry about doing (A)' in English.

なくてもいい is a combination of the auxiliary verb ない in its conjunction form, with てもいい.

In order to make this phrase sound even more casual, the adverbial particle も may be omitted. This does not change the nuance at all, but will sound a bit more friendly (when used with people that you know well).

attributes.description: Differences between 「することはない」 and 「しなくてもいい」
See examples with なくてもいい
Don't Have to ~（なくてもいい）

attributes.body: なくてもいい means there is no obligation to do something, like the English 'you don't have to (A)' (or literally, 'it's okay even without').  For example, 食べなくてもいい means 'You don't have to eat it.' In contrast, てはならない expresses prohibition, like 'must not (A)' or 'cannot (A)'. For example, 食べてはならない means 'You must not eat it.'.

ことはない and なくてもいい can overlap when expressing 'There is no need to...' or 'You don't have to...' For example, 心配することはない and 心配しなくてもいい both mean 'There's no need to worry.' However, ことはない can also be used to express that something never happens. For example, 彼と話すことはない means 'I never talk to him,' which is not a use for なくてもいい.

first_relatable.title: ことはない
first_relatable.meaning: There is no need to, Never happens

attributes.body: なくてはいけない expresses obligation or necessity, saying something 'must' or 'needs to' be done. なくてもいい has the opposite meaning, saying that one doesn't have to do something (literally, 'it's okay not to do'). For example, 食べなくてはいけない means '(You) must eat it', while 食べなくてもいい means '(You) don't have to eat it.'

なくてもいい means something is optional; 'it's okay not to (do something).' In contrast, てはいけない expresses prohibition; 'you must not' or 'cannot' do something. For example, 食べなくてもいい means 'It's okay not to eat it,' while 食べてはいけない means 'You must not eat it.' The first gives freedom; the second sets a rule.
